title: Synth SLA tradeoff needleplot notes
body:
Executive summary:

Quick internal notes from a small bench run (synth-storm generator) exploring SLA vs unit-cost at interactive scale (typical thin-client patterns). Goal: show a compact, visualizable needleplot-style view that product/console can surface: how small SLO shifts (p90/p99) move dollars-per-1k requests under three routing/priming strategies. Draft — rough numbers, noisy runs, meant for discussion.

Motivation / context:
- PM ask: short one-pager to help decide default SLO tiers for thin-client customers (mobile/web interactive).
- Observed in prod: microbursts and session priming cause disproportionate p99 variance; need a compact collateral that ties percentile targets to marginal $ spent.

Experiment design (synth-storm v0.3):
- Workloads: three session mixes representative of thin-client apps:
  1) Short-turn chat (median tokens per request = 40, taily replies) — labeled SHORT
  2) Command+Context (median tokens = 120, mixed prefix reuse) — labeled MID
  3) Rich assistant (median tokens = 420, longer KV cache life) — labeled LONG
- Traffic shape: steady baseline 200 qps + controlled microburst of 1500 qps for 30s every 10 minutes (to exercise warm/fallback behavior).
- Routing/priming strategies tested:
  A) Fast-path only: always route to smallest-latency variant, no prewarm
  B) Prewarm-on-sustain: prewarm instance after 5s sustained spike (reduces cold-starts but costs steady prewarm cycles)
  C) Adaptive-prefetch: predictive KV prefetch for reuse with lightweight slotization (lower token cost on long contexts)
- Models/stack: gpt-small-ish quant profile; runtime config: continuous batching enabled, KV cache hit modeled with 0.7 hit for LONG when prefetch used.

Metrics & cost model:
- Latency: p50, p90, p99 (ms) measured at gateway-observed end-to-end (client to first token).
- Unit cost: dollars per 1k requests (dollars/1k) approximated from GPU-second amortized + infra overhead. Conservative overhead added +20%.
- SLA penalty calculus: not applied here — we just show raw cost vs percentile tradeoff.

Raw aggregated table (median across 3 runs) — columns: scenario | p50 | p90 | p99 | $/1k
SHORT A | 48 ms | 110 ms | 640 ms | $1.12
SHORT B | 52 ms | 92 ms | 210 ms | $1.46
SHORT C | 50 ms | 98 ms | 180 ms | $1.28

MID A | 120 ms | 260 ms | 1200 ms | $2.40
MID B | 140 ms | 200 ms | 310 ms | $2.95
MID C | 130 ms | 210 ms | 260 ms | $2.62

LONG A | 410 ms | 860 ms | 2200 ms | $6.80
LONG B | 460 ms | 540 ms | 630 ms | $8.70
LONG C | 430 ms | 490 ms | 520 ms | $7.90

Interpretive needleplot ascii (conceptual): each row is scenario, markers show p90 (o) and p99 (|) relative to cost buckets on horizontal axis ($/1k). Axis ticks: $0 $2 $4 $6 $8 $10
SHORT A  : $1.12  [o......|................................]  (p90@1.12, p99@1.12 cost low but p99 high in time)
SHORT B  : $1.46  [.o....|..................................]  (p99 moved left dramatically)
SHORT C  : $1.28  [.o...|...................................]

MID A    : $2.40  [..o.............|........................]
MID B    : $2.95  [...o......|.............................]
MID C    : $2.62  [...o......|............................]

LONG A   : $6.80  [........o..............|................]
LONG B   : $8.70  [..........o.....|......................]
LONG C   : $7.90  [.........o.....|.......................]

Notes on the ascii: horizontal positioning approximates $/1k (left-right) and vertical density implies the latency gap between p90 and p99 (needle length). The goal: show that small increases in $/1k can collapse a long p99 tail for many session shapes — especially for strategies that invest in prewarming or predictive prefetch.

Key takeaways (working):
- Prewarm (B) reduces extreme p99 much more than it increases p50 — for SHORT and MID it collapses the tail by 2x–6x at a modest $/1k increase. Useful default for consumer thin-client SLO offering.
- Adaptive-prefetch (C) sits between A and B: slightly cheaper than B with p99 close to B for MID/LONG (where cache helps); for SHORT the benefit is lower.
- For LONG contexts, the marginal cost of chasing p99 is high due to sustained GPU time per request; prefetch helps but the cost delta remains material. Consider tiering: give LONG-heavy tenants higher committed capacity (Dedicated) or softer p99 guarantees.
- Microburst behavior drives most of the p99 delta. If we can reduce burst admission or shape earlier (client-side backpressure or edge buffering), the dollars-to-p99 curve flattens.

Detailed oddities observed / raw signals:
- One run showed LONG A p99 spike to ~4800 ms during a concurrent infra maintenance window — flagged but excluded from medians.
- Prewarm B showed steady 3% higher baseline infra CPU usage (control-plane), plausible cost allocation hit not fully captured by $/1k model.
- Prefetch C efficacy correlates strongly with session inter-arrival autocorrelation; more bursty but repeatable sessions see higher KV hit improvement.

Recommendations for console collateral / productization:
- Build a compact widget: "Needleplot — choose your SLO" that overlays p90/p99 vs $/1k for the customer's observed session mix (SHORT/MID/LONG). Allow toggles for routing strategy (fast-path / prewarm / adaptive).
- Default tier: prewarm (B) for consumer-facing thin-client with SLO p99 <= 300 ms. Flag customers with LONG mixes toward Dedicated guidance.
- Add a "what we measured" link that shows raw ascii tables and 95% CI. For now this doc is the seed for that content.

Open questions / next runs:
- Run with more model variants (higher compute-per-token) to check cost curvature — our run used a single model class.
- Add admission control shapings (edge-buffering) as a fourth strategy and re-evaluate microburst p99 benefit.
- Formalize cost model to include prewarm steady-state charge (we used amortized GPU seconds but need to separate idle prewarm cost).

Notes to self / TODOs:
- Share with SRE (Alex) to verify prewarm control-plane CPU overhead estimate.
- Ask Product (Priya) whether a 300 ms p99 is the right consumer target or if 500 ms acceptable for certain geos.
- Add chart export hooks in console prototype (needleplot svg + ascii fallback).

Appendix — quick run commands (synth-storm):
- ./synth-storm --profile thin-short --qps 200 --burst 1500 --burst-interval 600 --runs 3 --report needle-csv
- postproc: python tools/needle-compile.py --input runs/* --agg median --out ascii-needle.txt

Raw quick links: CONFLUENCE-4321 (reference), JIRA-INF-9823 (prewarm infra story), PR#1784 (runtime changes for predictive-prefetch).

End of notes — rough and opinionated, meant to seed a small internal working brief for console designers and product.
